trick: The empirical formula is always found the same way: divide the percentage of each element by its atomic mass, then divide every answer by the smallest of them. Percentage, divide by mass, divide by smallest — three steps, every time.

video.query: mole concept empirical and molecular formula class 11 chemistry

data.prompt: Find an empirical formula, one step at a time.
data.problem: A compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

steps.ask: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass. What do you get?
steps.why: 40/12 = 3.33, 6.7/1 = 6.7 and 53.3/16 = 3.33. These are the relative numbers of moles.

steps.ask: Now divide each by the smallest of the three.
So what is the empirical formula?
steps.why: CH2O. Note that this is the empirical formula only: glucose, C6H12O6, has the same one, which is why a molecular mass is needed to go further.

trick: Every gas law is the ideal gas equation with something held constant. Hold temperature and you get Boyle, hold pressure and you get Charles, hold volume and you get Gay-Lussac. Learn PV = nRT and derive the rest rather than memorising four laws.

video.query: gas laws Boyle Charles ideal gas equation class 11 chemistry

data.prompt: Choose the right relation for each gas law.

items.why: Pressure and volume are inversely proportional at fixed temperature: squeeze a gas and the pressure rises.
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature. T must be in kelvin — using Celsius here is the standard mistake.
n is the number of moles, not the mass in grams. If you are given grams, divide by the molar mass first.
Each gas in a mixture exerts the pressure it would exert alone, and those pressures simply add.

trick: Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point because every bond is the same length and they all break at once. Amorphous solids soften over a range because their bonds vary. If a question mentions a definite melting point, it is crystalline.

video.query: solid state crystalline amorphous unit cell class 11 chemistry

data.prompt: One of these is not a crystalline solid. Which, and why?
data.because: The other four have their particles in a regular repeating lattice, so each has a sharp melting point and a definite geometry. Glass is amorphous: its particles are disordered, it softens over a range instead of melting at one temperature, and it is sometimes described as a supercooled liquid. Note that quartz and glass are both silicon dioxide — the difference is arrangement, not composition.

trick: Hydrogen sits awkwardly in the periodic table because it behaves like two families at once: it loses an electron like an alkali metal and gains one like a halogen. Every question about its position is really about that double resemblance.

video.query: hydrogen isotopes hydrides hard and soft water class 11 chemistry

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about hydrogen.

items.statement: Hydrogen resembles both the alkali metals and the halogens.
items.why: It has one valence electron like an alkali metal, and needs one more to fill its shell like a halogen. That is why its position is debated.

items.statement: Deuterium and tritium are isotopes of hydrogen.
items.why: Protium has no neutron, deuterium one and tritium two. Tritium is radioactive.

items.statement: Hard water lathers easily with soap.
items.why: Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts which form a scum with soap. It is soft water that lathers well.

items.statement: Hydrogen peroxide acts only as an oxidising agent.
items.why: It can act as both an oxidising and a reducing agent, which is why it is used to bleach and also to reduce in some reactions.

items.statement: Temporary hardness can be removed by boiling.
items.why: Boiling decomposes the bicarbonates into insoluble carbonates. Permanent hardness, from sulphates and chlorides, needs washing soda or an ion exchanger.

trick: The s-block metals are so reactive that none is found free in nature, and reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron gets further from the nucleus. That single rule predicts almost everything, including why caesium reacts violently with water and lithium only fizzes.

trick: The group number tells you the valence electrons: group 13 has three, group 14 four, group 15 five. And the first element of every p-block group behaves oddly compared with the rest, because it is small and has no d orbitals — boron, carbon and nitrogen are all exceptions to their own families.
